newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - China signals buying interest.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - China signals buying interest.

text.p: Strong buy signals from China are seen providing the new month trading in Middle East and regional crudes with a firm start this week, traders said on Monday.
March trading in Oman has already started strongly and the loss of production from Australian crudes is underpinning the regional light sweet market and its benchmark Tapis crude.
An industry price marker set a blistering $26.18 per barrel for Tapis last week, adding 85 cents per barrel from its week-earlier quotation.

The high middle distillate yielding Tapis has already achieved a premium over paper swaps values of $1.75 per barrel -- its highest in more than a year -- taking outright wet values to their highest since the Gulf conflict at $27.00 per barrel.
But some traders said the price was now too high, when considered against the price of gas oil at $31.60 per barrel and kerosene at $32.75.
"You just can't work it at that level," one trader said, referring to refining margins.
However, Tapis is underpinned by the closure of Australia's 90,000 barrels per day (bpd) Cossack and 70,000 bpd Griffin fields for much of the last two weeks -- disconnected to avoid two cyclones.
The shutdowns have resulted in nine-day shipping delays at the fields and forced some Australian refineries to delay output schedules.
Replacement or fill-in crudes like Kutubu and Gippsland are in tight supply -- exacerbating the refineries problems.

Traders said they would expect a price reaction later this week or next as trading picks up after the New Year. February Tapis paper rose last week more than 70 cents per barrel to $25.30 per barrel, but futures prices were a strong influence.
"I would expect prices to rise, not just because of Australia, but because if you look at the overall, what could replace them," one Australia-based trader said.
But strong buying interest from China seems to be a major factor supporting prices as regional crudes head into February trading and Middle East grades head into March trading.

It signalled strong import interest for crude earlier this month. The China Daily on January 4 quoted Sinopec president, Sheng Huaren, saying "surging demand for finished oil and relatively stable supply of onshore oil have forced refineries to look into overseas markets."

Already, China was heard buying two Oman cargoes at MPM +31 and +32 cents -- a significant increase in price over February. Oman February went out around MPM +30 cents, but the Dubai/Oman differentials widened for March by 18 cents.
"I expected a strong month, but not so early," one Oman seller said.
An offsetting factor is expectations among traders that China is importing as many as three very large crude carriers of West African grades for late February and March arrival.

But medium grades, like Oman, Dubai and Masila, could also find support from Japan and South Korea downgrading from light grades because of moderate winter temperatures and a move into spring schedules.
Traders said Iran has also cut some allocations to Japan in February after over commiting to the west -- another supporting factor for medium grades.
The benchmark Indonesia grade, Minas, went out in January just below ICP +90 cents, but traders said talk was around plus $1.00 for February, owing to expected Chinese buying.
However, with Chinese New Year fast approaching in February, China's buying interest may start to slow as it covers its holiday requirements.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
